messages.body_plain:
I have a similar question / issue. I want to save my IIFs and ICCs to a folder. I also want to do this for each item individually rather than in a matrix or facet form. I can do that easily with a for loop with information

Theta <- seq(-4,4, by = .1)
nitems <- ncol(irtdata)

for(i in 1:nitems){
  info <- iteminfo(extract.item(model, i), Theta)
  png(file = paste("Model 1 ", names(irtdata)[[i]], " Info.png", sep=""))
    plot(Theta, info, type = "l", main = paste("Information for ",
                names(irtdata)[[i]], sep = ""), ylab = "Information", xlab = "Theta")
    lines(Theta, info, col = "steelblue")
  dev.off()
}

However, similar loops create blank plots for ICCs. I believe the plots are blank for the same reason the above poster mentioned. For reference I have tried the following methods which produce the same resulting blank plots. The loops without the png statement simply don't create a graphical object.

for(i in 1:nitems){
  png(file = paste("Model ", iteration, " ", names(irtdata)[[i]], " ICC.png", sep=""))
  plot(model, type = "trace", which.items = i)
  dev.off()
}

for(i in 1:nitems){
  png(file = paste("Model ", iteration, " ", names(irtdata)[[i]], " ICC.png", sep=""))
  itemplot(model, i, type = "trace")
  dev.off()
}

Do you know how we can get the ICC's to plot in their own window? itemplot can be run manually for every item in the set which works for say 5 or 10 items but for more than 20 it becomes tedious.

Best,
Scott

messages.subject: relaxing constraints in latent regression?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phil,

I have been working with a colleague using the mirt package (version 1.10) to estimate IRT models and latent regressions.  Thanks very much for putting together such a powerful and user-friendly package.  We have run into an issue that we haven’t been able to figure out and are hoping you can provide some guidance.  The simplest scenario in which we are having trouble is the following.  We have a 2PL model with known item parameters.  The parameters were calibrated assuming a N(0,1) distribution for \theta.  We are then using mirt() to estimate a latent regression on a single dichotomous covariate X.  Because the item parameters are fixed and known during this estimation, it seems that we should be able to identify three parameters of the latent regression \theta = X\beta + \epsilon: an intercept, \beta, and var(\epsilon).  E[\epsilon] is fixed at zero.  However, all mirt() syntax variations we have tried are resulting in only two estimated parameters: \beta and var(\epsilon).  The “estimated” intercept is always reported as being fixed at zero.  For example, we even tried manually changing est=TRUE for “F1_(Intercept)” in the “pars” structure and suppressing an intercept and trying to estimate coefficients for both groups for the dichotomous variable.  We also tried letting the mean of the latent factor be estimated freely, but still get a fixed zero.  Do you have any ideas for how we can relax the constraint on the intercept and get three estimated parameters from this latent regression?  Thanks for your time and consideration.

J.R.

Hi Scott and others,

One of the strengths of R is the vectorization that essentially eliminates the need to use 'for' loops. R's behind the scenes stuff uses quite efficient 'for' loops, so when you specify a 'for' loop in R syntax you're essentially running double the number of loops, which can be very, very slow. I had a problem similar to yours that I resolved using the 'apply' family of base functions in R, which is reproduced below:

# these are the titles you want to appear at the top of each item plot
titles= list("Excited", "Enthused", "Bored", "Stressed", "Nervous", "Relaxed", "Calm", "Serene", "Alert", "Satisifed", "Content", "Upset", "Dissatisfied", "Happy", "Tired", "Tense","Gloomy")

# this a list of of the item names in the dataset to be plotted.
item.names.pre = list("excited.pre.scored", "enthused.pre.scored", "bored.pre.scored", "stressed.pre.scored", "nervous.pre.scored", "relaxed.pre.scored", "calm.pre.scored", "serene.pre.scored", "alert.pre.scored", "satisifed.pre.scored", "content.pre.scored", "upset.pre.scored", "dissatisfied.pre.scored", "happy.pre.scored", "tired.pre.scored", "tense.pre.scored","gloomy.pre.scored")

# This is a custom function that acts as a wrapper for mirt's itemplot() function.
# I've set this to create PDFs but you can easily modify it to use PNGs as you've done above
# just change the function from pdf() to png()
plots = function(fit, item, title, time){
> > #fit is the mirt fit object
> > #item is the list created above that has the names of the items to be plotted
> > #title is the list created above that contains the plot titles
> > #you can ignore the time argument, I added this because I have pre/post versions of these items,
> > #so I needed to dynamically reference the appropriate folder
> >
> > #creates the location of where to save the plots, dynamically titles each plot using the 'title' list
> > pdf(file=paste0("path/to/file", time, "/", title, ".pdf") )
> >
> > #creates a mirt itemplot() object, will be used later to set specific features of the plots (e.g., axes names)
> > plt = itemplot(fit, item, rot=list(xaxis=-55, yaxis=30, zaxis=25), main=title) # add arguments here to get info traces instead of ICCs
> >
> > #references the item plot object plt and adds names to the x and y axes
> > #you can find the specific plot item characteristics using str(plt)
> > plt$panel.args.common$xlab = "Approach" # you can add an x-axis title here
> > plt$panel.args.common$ylab = "Avoid" # you can add an y-axis title here
> >
> > #prints plot to PDF
> > print(plt)
> >
> > dev.off()
}

Now, the function above is pretty basic but the way you call that function is the strength of R. Rather having to use a 'for' loop to go through all the items, use simply us mapply() that will call the plots() function above once for each element found in the 'item.names.pre' and 'titles' arguments below. These apply() functions are not that intuitive but you can get a detailed explanation and examples using ?apply. The apply() family of functions are much, much, much faster than for loops so there will be an increasing benefit as the size of the items to plot increases.

mapply(function(item, title, time) plots(chaffect.fit.pre.dom, item, title, time), item.names.pre, titles, "Pre")

Please let me know if you have any questions about the above and I'll try to answer them to the best of my ability.

HTH,
Garett

messages.body_plain:
Hi J.R.,

On Wed, Jul 1, 2015 at 6:06 PM, J.R. Lockwood <jloc...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello Phil,
>
>
> I have been working with a colleague using the mirt package (version 1.10) to estimate IRT models and latent regressions.  Thanks very much for putting together such a powerful and user-friendly package.  We have run into an issue that we haven’t been able to figure out and are hoping you can provide some guidance.  The simplest scenario in which we are having trouble is the following.  We have a 2PL model with known item parameters.  The parameters were calibrated assuming a N(0,1) distribution for θ.  We are then using mirt() to estimate a latent regression on a single dichotomous covariate X.  Because the item parameters are fixed and known during this estimation, it seems that we should be able to identify three parameters of the latent regression θ = Xβ + ε: an intercept, β, and var(ε).  E[ε] is fixed at zero.

Is there any reason these should be treated as fixed and known? The latent regression model can estimate these simultaneously along with the latent regression effects.

> However, all mirt() syntax variations we have tried are resulting in only two estimated parameters: β and var(ε).  The “estimated” intercept is always reported as being fixed at zero.  For example, we even tried manually changing est=TRUE for “F1Intercept” in the “pars” structure and suppressing an intercept and trying to estimate coefficients for both groups for the dichotomous variable.

That's true largely out of redundancy. Because the design you are speaking of only has two levels, the X design matrix should only have one coefficient to separate the means of the dichotomous effect. Therefore, even if the intercept was estimated here, it wouldn't tell you anything more than what you already want to know. So internally the intercept is always set to 0, and is not possible to freely estimate.

I think in this circumstance it makes more sense to free the latent variance parameter though, so you can see how much variability is 'explained' by the fixed regression effect before and after the explanatory effect is included. There should only be two parameters estimated in a latent regression with a dichotomous predictor: the β coefficient from the dummy term in X, and the variance of ε (which coincides with the variance of Θ here).

> We also tried letting the mean of the latent factor be estimated freely, but still get a fixed zero.  Do you have any ideas for how we can relax the constraint on the intercept and get three estimated parameters from this latent regression?  Thanks for your time and consideration.

If you are interested in these types of models further with mirt, I'd recommend looking into a paper which was recently released in JEM....which apparently I forgot to update the citation information for (uses the mixedmirt function in the package):

Chalmers, R. P. (2015). Extended Mixed-Effects Item Response Models with the MH-RM Algorithm
Journal of Educational Measurement, 52, 200-222.

It talks about various ways to model explanatory IRT models, and should be more than enough to help you along (also supports latent regression models....just not true multilevel IRT models just yet). Cheers.

Phil

Hi Phill,

I am using the mirt package within an RScript on my application that is called through command line as part of the workflow. However, when the overall execution time of the RScript takes ~4s, 2 of them are only loading up the lattice package, which as I understand serves only for visualization purposes. Since this step is run many times during the workflow (and the RScript has to load the packages everytime) this causes too much overhead.

messages.subject: Re: Monotonically decreasing function
messages.body_plain:
The guessing parameters are stored as logits, and -1.5 was just my selected location as an example. If, for instance, you wanted the g values to be centered around .2, then you would need to change -1.5 to log(.2/(1-.2)) = -1.386. The 3 is the variance of this prior, where a smaller value means a stronger prior (larger values make it more diffuse). Justifying how tight this prior should be is a matter of personal or prior information collected from previous literature; such is the issue with all Bayesian applications, and here it's no different.

And yes, 5 is referring to the 5th item. See ?mirt.model for more information on how to specify additional items.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I am no longer work on the IRT project. No need to answer the questions below. Thanks.

I have been working on IRT calibration for Science Assessments for Grade 7-11. Although I have been reading some papers on IRT analysis, I still feel puzzled about applying IRT outputs to test measurement/development. I have a series of questions regarding the interpretation of IRT outputs or IRT concepts. I know you are super busy now. When you have free time, could you help me? Thanks so much.

1.       Some items are constructed responses with score of 0 or 1. In the IRT model, I treated them as binary data. However, they are more difficult than multiple-choice with 1 correct answer. Is there any methods/algorithm in MIRT I can use to take this fact into consideration? (i.e., a prior norm distribution of g)

2.. Some items were multiple-choice with multiple correct answers, but they were scored as 1 or 0. Again, they are more difficult than multiple-choice with 1 correct answer. Is there any methods/algorithm in MIRT I can use to take this fact into consideration to make more accurate estimate of a and b parameters?

3.  For model fit, I always got significant p values for X2 because of large sample size (N > 1000). So I examined RMSEA, TLI, and CFT values. For one assessment, RMSEA was less than 0.05, indication a good fit. However, both TLI and CFT was less than 0.90, indicating poor fit. In this scenario, how should I determine if the model is good fit or not? Or is there alternative method for determining model fit?

4.  For model fit, if we don’t have model fit at all, can I still use estimated a, b, c for item calibration? Or Should I must have a model fit before any item calibration?

5.  For factor analysis, both parallel analysis and exploratory analysis indicated multiple factors for one assessment (i.e., 5 factors), but the data fitted a 1-fact 3PL model. How is this possible?

6.  For item fit analysis, the items with p > 0.5 indicate a good fit. For most of my assessments, although model fit, but many items did not fit. For example, 4 out of 24 items did not fit for one assessment. How should I interpret these results?

7.  For testing local independence, I examined the LD and Q3 values and found that Q3 revealed a lot more problematic item pairs. Based on my research, I used the criteria that any item pair with LD greater than 0.1 or Q3 greater than 0.1 were identified as local dependence. One research article indeed suggested that Q3 is more sensitive than other LD indices.  But if the model is unidimensional (not in absolute term) and I got many related item pairs, how should I interpret this outcome?

Thanks so much for helping.

Best regards,

Sue

IRT recognizes that some areas are measured better than others by tests, and therefore that information gets included in the conditional reliability estimates given the latent trait (e.g. plot(mod, type = 'rxx')). I have a series of questions regarding the interpretation of IRT outputs or IRT concepts. I know you are super busy now. When you have free time, could you help me? Thanks so much.
>

> 1.S1. Some items are constructed responses with score of 0 or 1. In the IRT model, I treated them as binary data. However, they are more difficult than multiple-choice with 1 correct answer. Is there any methods/algorithm in MIRT I can use to take this fact into consideration? (i.e., a prior norm distribution of g)
Not sure what you mean by more difficult here. It sounds like the items are more important from a raw scoring perspective, but IRT generally doesn't care about that. It will only try to quantify how well items relate to the latent trait, so the importance gets factored in automatically.

>
> 2.
>
> 3.      2. Some items were multiple-choice with multiple correct answers, but they were scored as 1 or 0. Again, they are more difficult than multiple-choice with 1 correct answer. Is there any methods/algorithm in MIRT I can use to take this fact into consideration to make more accurate estimate of a and b parameters?

See above.

>
>
>
> 4.       3. For model fit, I always got significant p values for X2 because of large sample size (N > 1000). So I examined RMSEA, TLI, and CFT values. For one assessment, RMSEA was less than 0.05, indication a good fit. However, both TLI and CFT was less than 0.90, indicating poor fit. In this scenario, how should I determine if the model is good fit or not? Or is there alternative method for determining model fit?

These are rules of thumb of course, and for categorical data standards have not been set. Use them as descriptors and indications of the model misfitting. These numbers are probably fine.
>
>
>
> 5.       4. For model fit, if we don’t have model fit at all, can I still use estimated a, b, c for item calibration? Or Should I must have a model fit before any item calibration?

Model fit implies that the test as a whole doesn't seem well predicted (or at least the covariances between the items are predicted well). Individual items can still be useful after careful screening.

>
>
>
> 6.       5. For factor analysis, both parallel analysis and exploratory analysis indicated multiple factors for one assessment (i.e., 5 factors), but the data fitted a 1-fact 3PL model. How is this possible?

Not quite sure what you mean. But did your parallel analysis use tetrachoric correlations? There may be difficulty factors present, and even at that the methodology for exploratory factor analysis is approximate at best.
>
>
>
> 7.       6. For item fit analysis, the items with p > 0.5 indicate a good fit. For most of my assessments, although model fit, but many items did not fit. For example, 4 out of 24 items did not fit for one assessment. How should I interpret these results?

Check what's going on with the itemGAM() function. It should give you an indication of what's going on in the probability functions, which may help you diagnose the problem.

>
>
>
> 8.       7. For testing local independence, I examined the LD and Q3 values and found that Q3 revealed a lot more problematic item pairs. Based on my research, I used the criteria that any item pair with LD greater than 0.1 or Q3 greater than 0.1 were identified as local dependence. One research article indeed suggested that Q3 is more sensitive than other LD indices.  But if the model is unidimensional (not in absolute term) and I got many related item pairs, how should I interpret this outcome?

Q3 is more problematic because it uses secondary estimates of factor scores, whereas LD integrates over the distributions. Also, it really depends on the magnitude and clusters of the related items. If no clusters are formed, the covariation could just be random association and not be a huge problem. Clusters on the other hand indicate a residual factor which may be useful to model (you could factor analyse the residual correlation matrix to see if that helps.....the same could be done via M2() as well).

Phil
